questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify whether a duty is ministerial and therefore reachable by mandamus
questions.stem: The projection sheet for the eastern district carries a marginal note asking whether a court may compel a surveyor to remeasure a boundary that the statute lets the surveyor judge.

options.text: Yes, because the statute mentions remeasurement and so the duty is ministerial.
options.misconception: treats any statutory mention as a ministerial duty

options.text: Yes, because a delay in remeasuring the boundary harms the landowners awaiting it.
options.misconception: grounds compulsion in the harm of delay

options.text: No, because no court may ever order a surveyor to do anything at all.
options.misconception: denies mandamus entirely

options.text: No, because the writ reaches ministerial duties and the statute leaves the surveyor discretion.

questions.explanation: A writ of mandamus compels ministerial duties only, and a statute that lets the surveyor judge the boundary creates discretion. The mention of a duty and the harm of delay do not change that classification.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statute leaves the officer a choice.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State when judgment may be entered for the party who did not move
questions.stem: The sheet index asks the legal desk to explain when judgment may be entered for the party who did not move.

answer.exemplar: A court may enter summary judgment for the defendant only where the plaintiff has failed to show a genuine dispute of material fact, so that no reasonable person could find for the plaintiff on the evidence viewed in that party's favor. Credibility is not decided on the papers, and a plaintiff's mere allegations are not enough unless supported by evidence.

questions.explanation: Judgment for the defendant follows from the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact in the plaintiff's favour. Credibility cannot be resolved on paper, and unsupported allegations are not enough to survive the motion.
questions.hint: One test, applied to the plaintiff's showing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the activist and restrained labels describe

stimulus.body: A marginal note in the projection manual states that a ruling is called activist when it is said to have substituted the judge's own view for the enacted law, and restrained when it is said to have confined itself to the text without stretching it.

questions.stem: The manual's marginal note treats the labels as describing which of the following.

options.text: The political leaning of the panel that issued the ruling, which is the usual shorthand in practice.
options.misconception: reduces the labels to the panel's politics

options.text: The size of the margin of error on the sheet, since precision is the cartographer's concern.
options.misconception: turns a legal label into a drafting convention

options.text: The degree of interpretive judgment the court exercised in construing the enacted text.
The length of the written opinion, since longer reasoning is thought to be bolder reasoning.
options.misconception: ties the label to the length of the opinion

questions.explanation: The labels describe how much interpretive judgment a court exercised and whether it stayed within the enacted words. Political leaning, drafting preferences, and opinion length do not decide whether a ruling is activist or restrained.
questions.hint: Read the note for what the label is said to accuse.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of an overrule on earlier reliance

stimulus.body: A cartographer's case note records that a reviewing court overruled one of its own earlier decisions on a question of survey law, and that the earlier decision had been followed by surveyors in several states for a decade before the change.

questions.stem: The note turns on which proposition about the effect of the overrule.

options.text: The new rule governs later cases, while the surveys already made in reliance on the old rule are not disturbed.
The new rule governs later cases, and every survey already completed under the old rule is void.
options.misconception: makes the overrule void past reliance

options.text: The old rule survives until every state surveyor has adopted the new one, so the change waits.
options.misconception: delays the overrule until state adoption

options.text: The overrule has no effect at all, because a court is bound by every decision it has issued.
options.misconception: makes a court forever bound by its own rulings

questions.explanation: An overrule changes the rule for cases that come after it, while completed work done in reliance on the earlier rule is left alone. Reliance is the reason earlier results endure, and adoption by other states is irrelevant.
questions.hint: New rule forward, completed work preserved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State who a court-ordered remedy may reach and what it must rest on
questions.stem: A survey dispute file asks two things about the relief sought: who it must reach, and what it must rest on.

options.text: It must reach every landowner in the county; it must rest on what the surveyor judged equitable.
options.misconception: pairs county-wide reach with subjective fairness

options.text: It must reach the state agency too; it must rest on the agency's enforcement priorities.
options.misconception: makes agency priorities the basis of relief

options.text: It must reach only the parties to the suit; it must rest on the claims and the proof in the record.
It must reach the parties to the suit; it must rest on whatever relief the parties request.
options.misconception: makes the request itself the measure of relief

questions.explanation: Relief runs against the parties to the judgment and must be supported by the claims and the proof. A court cannot reach non-parties, and the size or shape of the remedy is not set by fairness or by the request.
questions.hint: Parties and record, not fairness or preference.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Apply the rule of constitutional avoidance to a statutory construction
questions.stem: The legend on a projected sheet asks how a court should read a statute whose broad reading would collide with the constitution.

options.text: It should read it broadly, because a statute is construed to give the government the widest power.
options.misconception: presumes breadth favours the government

options.text: It should read it broadly, because constitutional questions are easier to answer later.
options.misconception: defers the constitution for procedural ease

options.text: It should read it both ways and pick the one that is more convenient to enforce.
options.misconception: makes enforcement convenience the test

options.text: It should read it narrowly if a reasonable narrower reading avoids the constitutional problem.

questions.explanation: A court adopts a reasonable construction that avoids the constitutional conflict and decides the case on the statute. It reaches the constitutional question only where the statute cannot avoid the problem.
questions.hint: Prefer the reading that keeps the case off the constitution.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a question unsuitable for decision for lack of a standard
questions.stem: The projection office asks what makes a question unsuitable for a court's decision because there is no standard to apply.

answer.exemplar: A question may be treated as a political question when there is no judicially manageable standard for the court to apply, such as where the issue is committed to another branch by the constitution or where a statutory standard is so broad that the court cannot say what the law requires. Courts are reluctant to make such a finding, because it leaves the claim without a remedy.

questions.explanation: The absence of a workable legal standard is what makes a question non-justiciable, whether the constitution commits it elsewhere or a statute is too indefinite to apply. Courts hesitate because the consequence is dismissal without a remedy.
questions.hint: No standard, no judicial answer.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what happens when a consent decree reaches the end of its term

stimulus.body: A note in the survey archive records that a consent decree entered in a boundary dispute provided that its terms would run for a fixed period and that, upon expiry, the obligations it imposed would end without further order of the court.

questions.stem: According to the note, what happens to the decree when its stated period ends.

options.text: It continues in force, because a court order does not expire on its own terms.
options.misconception: denies that a decree can carry an expiry date

options.text: Its terms end on the stated date, and no further order is needed to bring them to a close.
It continues in force until a party moves, because the expiry clause has no legal effect.
options.misconception: makes an expiry clause unenforceable

options.text: It is void from the outset, because a decree may not provide for its own termination.
options.misconception: denies that a decree may set an end date

questions.explanation: A consent decree may fix its own term, and on expiry the obligations it imposed simply end without any further order. It is not void for having an expiry date, nor does it continue until someone asks for its termination.
questions.hint: The decree can set its own end date.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the ministerial-duty test to a recorder's refusal to act

stimulus.body: A sheet note describes a county recorder who is required by statute to record any deed presented to the office, and who has refused to record a deed because the accompanying tax receipt could not be produced.

questions.stem: The recorder's step described in the note runs into which difficulty.

options.text: If the statute leaves the recorder discretion to decide what supporting documents suffice, the writ is unavailable.
The difficulty is that a county recorder is a state officer, so no federal court could ever act.
options.misconception: makes the writ depend on the officer's level of government

options.text: The difficulty is that the deed cannot be recorded at all while the tax question is unresolved.
options.misconception: converts a review question into a tax dispute

options.text: The difficulty is that recording is ministerial only after the recorder has first refused in writing.
options.misconception: invents a written-refusal prerequisite

questions.explanation: The writ reaches ministerial duties, so it turns on whether the statute leaves the recorder discretion over supporting documents. The officer's level of government, the underlying tax question, and a written refusal are not the obstacles.
questions.hint: Ask whether the recorder still has a choice.

questions.learningObjective: State who must show what and what the court may not do
questions.stem: The projection office asks two things about judgment for the defendant: who must show what, and what the court must not do.

options.text: The defendant must show the claim has merit; and the court may weigh the competing affidavits.
options.misconception: puts the merit burden on the defendant

options.text: The defendant must show the claim has merit; and the court may judge the credibility of the witnesses.
options.misconception: allows credibility findings on the papers

options.text: The plaintiff must show a genuine dispute of material fact; and the court may not weigh evidence or credibility.
The plaintiff must show the claim has merit; and the court may draw whatever inferences favour the defendant.
options.misconception: substitutes the merits for the summary judgment test

questions.explanation: Judgment for the defendant is proper only where the plaintiff has failed to show a genuine dispute of material fact, and the court may neither weigh evidence nor judge credibility. The burden of persuasion at trial does not migrate onto the papers.
questions.hint: The plaintiff must show dispute; the court may not weigh.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a ruling gets labelled activist in ordinary argument
questions.stem: A cartographer asks which description best captures why a ruling gets labelled activist in ordinary legal argument.

options.text: The ruling is activist because it produced an outcome the commentator disapproved of.
options.misconception: treats the label as a verdict on the outcome

options.text: The ruling is activist because the panel was newly appointed and lacked familiarity with the statute.
options.misconception: attributes activism to the panel's tenure

options.text: The ruling is activist because the opinion was longer than the opinions in the same series.
options.misconception: uses opinion length as a proxy for activism

options.text: The ruling is activist because the reasoning is said to reach beyond what the enacted text supports.

questions.explanation: The charge is that the court went beyond the enacted law in construing it, which is a claim about the reasoning rather than the result. Appointment, familiarity, and opinion length say nothing about the source of the rule applied.
questions.hint: The label accuses the reasoning, not the result.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court changing its rule explains itself at length
questions.stem: The sheet compiler asks why a court that changes its rule after parties have relied on the old one usually explains itself at length.

answer.exemplar: Because the change comes with a duty to explain. The court must say which decision it is displacing, why the earlier reasoning no longer holds, and how the new rule applies to the case before it, so that parties who relied on the old rule can see what the change means and adjust their conduct.

questions.explanation: An overruling decision must apply the new rule, justify displacing the old one, and engage the reasoning that supported it. That explanation is what lets parties who relied on the earlier rule see the change and adjust.
questions.hint: Explanation is part of the work of overruling.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the reach of a decree limited to the parties and the parcels in dispute

stimulus.body: A compilation note records that the decree entered after a boundary case was 'limited to the parties and to the parcels actually in dispute,' and that the surveyor who had surveyed the whole district in reliance on the earlier line was not bound.

questions.stem: The note supports which statement about the reach of the decree.

options.text: The decree binds every surveyor who relied on the earlier boundary line in the district.
options.misconception: extends the decree to those who merely relied on it

options.text: The decree binds the county because the county joined the case as an interested party.
options.misconception: assumes joinder of a county without record support

options.text: The decree has no effect because it failed to state the parcels it covered with precision.
options.misconception: makes imprecision fatal to the decree

options.text: The decree binds only the parties to the suit, and it does not reach a non-party surveyor.

questions.explanation: A decree binds the parties to the judgment and reaches only the parcels in dispute, so a non-party surveyor who relied on the earlier line is not bound. Nor does a party who never joined become subject to it.
questions.hint: A line others relied on is not automatically a line they are bound by.

questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Decide how a court should read a statute with two possible constructions

stimulus.body: A projection note records that a statute may be read either to cover a certain kind of survey or to exempt it, and that the broader reading would conflict with a settled constitutional rule about how that statute must be applied.

questions.stem: The note implies that the court should most likely do what.

options.text: Adopt the broader reading, because a statute should be given the greatest workable effect.
options.misconception: makes breadth the default interpretive rule

options.text: Adopt the narrower reading if it is reasonable, and decide the case on the statute alone.
Adopt the broader reading and let the challenge settle whether the conflict is real or imagined.
options.misconception: reaches the constitutional issue before trying the statute

options.text: Declare the statute ambiguous and send the question to the legislature for resolution.
options.misconception: sends a judicial question to the legislature

questions.explanation: Where a reasonable narrower reading avoids the constitutional conflict, the court adopts it and decides the case on the statute. It reaches the constitutional question only where the statute cannot avoid the problem.
questions.hint: Try the reading that keeps the constitution out of the case.

questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish non-justiciability from other grounds for refusing a claim
questions.stem: The projection office asks two things about a claim the court considers non-justiciable: what makes it so, and what follows.

options.text: It is non-justiciable because the claim is weak; and the court should dismiss it on the merits.
options.misconception: treats non-justiciability as a merits ruling

options.text: It is non-justiciable because the plaintiff has lost interest; and the court should dismiss it as moot.
options.misconception: conflates mootness with non-justiciability

options.text: It is non-justiciable because there is no standard to apply; and the court declines to decide it.
It is non-justiciable because the agency has not decided; and the court must remand for a decision.
options.misconception: turns the standard question into an exhaustion question

questions.explanation: A claim is non-justiciable because the court has no manageable standard to apply, so it declines to decide the merits. Weakness and lost interest raise different doctrines, and agency inaction is a route to review rather than a bar to it.
questions.hint: No standard to apply, so no decision to make.

questions.learningObjective: State what happens to a decree when its fixed term has run out
questions.stem: A records clerk asks what happens to the obligations in a consent decree once the fixed term it states has run out.

options.text: They end on the stated date, because a consent decree may provide for its own expiry.
They continue, because a decree must be modified by a further order before it ends.
options.misconception: requires a further order for the term to end

options.text: They continue indefinitely, because the decree is a judgment and judgments never lapse.
options.misconception: makes judgments immune to expiry by their terms

options.text: They are converted into damages, because the expiry is treated as a breach by the party.
options.misconception: turns expiry into a breach and damages

questions.explanation: A consent decree may set its own term, and the obligations it imposes end when that term expires without further proceedings. It is not converted into damages, nor does a judgment automatically endure forever.
questions.hint: The decree can name its own ending date.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the writ of mandamus is described as extraordinary
questions.stem: The survey handbook asks why the writ of mandamus is described as an extraordinary remedy.

answer.exemplar: Because it asks a court to order an official to act when the ordinary routes are closed, and it reaches only ministerial duties. The petitioner must show a clear and undeniable right and that no other adequate remedy exists, so the writ is reserved for unusual situations where a party would otherwise be left without a remedy.

questions.explanation: The writ is extraordinary because it demands the act of an official without any ordinary appeal and only where the duty is ministerial. Its narrow conditions protect both the official's discretion and the ordinary routes of review.
questions.hint: It bypasses the ordinary routes and reaches only fixed duties.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the test for judgment in favour of the defendant

stimulus.body: A drafting instruction states that a court may enter judgment for the defendant only where the plaintiff has failed to show a genuine dispute of material fact, that the court must draw all reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favour, and that the court may not weigh evidence or assess credibility.

questions.stem: The instruction supports which statement about judgment for the defendant.

options.text: The defendant is entitled to judgment whenever the court finds the plaintiff's allegations unconvincing.
options.misconception: substitutes unconvincing allegations for the test

options.text: The defendant is entitled to judgment whenever the plaintiff's evidence is merely thinner than the defendant's.
options.misconception: makes relative strength of evidence the test

options.text: The defendant is entitled to judgment only if the court finds for the defendant on the merits.
options.misconception: requires a merits finding for judgment on papers

options.text: The defendant is entitled to judgment only where the plaintiff has not shown a genuine dispute of material fact.

questions.explanation: The instruction's test is the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact in the plaintiff's favour, not the relative strength of the evidence or the judge's view of the allegations. A merits finding is not required on the papers.
questions.hint: One standard, and it favours the plaintiff on the papers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify why a narrow construction is described as restrained

stimulus.body: A marginal note records a case in which the court read a regulation narrowly and explained that the broad reading would impose duties the enabling statute did not authorise, and a commentary called the decision restrained.

questions.stem: The translator asks why the commentary used the word restrained here.

options.text: Because the court confined itself to what the enacted law authorised instead of extending it further.
Because the outcome favoured no party and so offended nobody in the dispute.
options.misconception: treats neutrality as the measure of restraint

options.text: Because the case was decided by a unanimous panel, which suggests a cautious court.
options.misconception: uses panel unanimity as the measure of restraint

options.text: Because the court avoided the constitutional question, which is always the restrained course.
options.misconception: makes constitutional avoidance the measure of restraint

questions.explanation: The label fits because the court stayed inside what the enacted law authorised rather than stretching it. An even outcome, panel unanimity, and avoidance of a constitutional question do not by themselves make a ruling restrained.
questions.hint: Ask whether the court stayed inside the enacted words.

questions.learningObjective: State the operation of a change of law on later cases and past acts
questions.stem: The compiler asks two things about a change of law after parties have acted on the earlier rule: what happens to the rule, and what happens to the past acts.

options.text: The old rule continues, because a court may not disturb anyone's reliance.
options.misconception: makes reliance a bar to overruling

options.text: The new rule governs later cases, and acts already done in reliance on the old rule are not undone.
The new rule governs all cases, and acts already done in reliance on the old rule are undone.
options.misconception: extends the overrule to completed reliance

options.text: The old rule governs all cases, and the court announces the change for future reference only.
options.misconception: announces a change without changing the law

questions.explanation: A change of law applies to cases that come after it, while completed acts done in reliance on the old rule are left undisturbed. Neither reliance nor the announcement alone determines which rule governs.
questions.hint: Forward for the law, backward for completed acts.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court cannot order a non-party officer to perform work
questions.stem: A title office asks why the court in a boundary case cannot order the county surveyor to re-survey the whole district at the plaintiffs' expense.

options.misconception: makes an elected office immune from orders

options.text: Because the court lacks the power to order any government officer to perform any duty.

options.misconception: makes prior agreement a precondition for relief

questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court prefers a construction that avoids a constitutional question
questions.stem: The map room asks why a court prefers to read a statute narrowly when a broader reading would raise a constitutional problem.

answer.exemplar: Because deciding the case on a reasonable narrower construction keeps the court from deciding a constitutional question it need not decide, which avoids a broader ruling than the controversy requires and avoids interference with the legislature. If no reasonable construction avoids the conflict, the court must reach the constitutional issue and say whether the statute is valid.

questions.explanation: Avoidance keeps the court within the controversy and leaves the constitutional question open where it can. Only where no reasonable construction avoids the conflict must the court decide the constitutional issue and rule on validity.
questions.hint: Deciding less is a virtue in a reviewing court.

questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Explain why opposing labels can attach to the same decision
questions.stem: The compiler asks why two courts applying the same statute can both claim the restrained label and the activist label for the same problem.

answer.exemplar: Because the labels turn on judgment about how far a court may go in construing ambiguous text, and reasonable judges can differ on that. Each side can fairly point to the text, the precedent, and the consequences to support its own view, which is why the charge is always argued from the reasoning rather than settled by a formula.

questions.explanation: The labels turn on contested judgments about interpretive reach, so different courts can defend opposite descriptions from the same materials. That is why the charge is always made from the reasoning rather than decided by any fixed formula.
questions.hint: The labels are arguments, and arguments can differ.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the situations reached by an overrule as stated in an opinion

stimulus.body: An editorial note records that the court overruled an earlier decision and stated that 'the rule announced today applies to cases arising after this decision, and we leave undisturbed the judgments already entered and the surveys already made in reliance on the earlier rule.'

questions.stem: The note's language indicates that the effect of the overrule reaches which situations.

options.text: Cases arising after the decision, while earlier judgments and completed surveys are left as they stand.
All cases, so that every earlier judgment must be reopened and every survey redone.
options.misconception: extends the overrule to all completed work

options.text: Only cases pending on appeal, because earlier judgments and completed surveys are permanent.
options.misconception: limits the new rule to pending appeals

options.text: No case at all, because the note states the change for information only.
options.misconception: reads the announcement as having no effect

questions.explanation: The quoted language applies the new rule to later cases while preserving earlier judgments and completed surveys, which is the ordinary effect of an overrule. It does not reopen concluded matters or leave the new rule inoperative.
questions.hint: Read the quoted sentence clause by clause.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a court could order relief binding only the owners who sued

stimulus.body: A land note describes a case in which two owners sued a surveyor over a boundary line, and the court ordered the line to be resurveyed and the cost to be shared equally between the two owners.

questions.stem: The note turns on why the court could order that relief.

options.text: Because the surveyor consented to the resurvey and so was bound by the consent.
options.misconception: makes a consent decree the source of the relief

options.text: Because the court thought an equal split was fair, and fairness guides the choice of remedy.
options.misconception: makes fairness the source of the remedy

options.text: Because the order bound only the owners, who were the parties to the suit and had the power to accept it.
Because every landowner in the district was given notice of the case and could have appeared.
options.misconception: treats notice to non-parties as sufficient

questions.explanation: The court could order relief because it bound only the parties, who were before it and could contest the terms. Consent by the surveyor and fairness in dividing costs are not what makes the order permissible, and notice to others does not bind them.
questions.hint: Ask who the order actually binds.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the statutory and constitutional questions in a statutory case
questions.stem: The map room asks two things about a case in which a statute can be read two ways and one reading avoids a constitutional problem.

options.text: First, decide the constitutional question; second, apply whichever reading the court prefers.
options.misconception: reverses the order and leaves the choice to preference

options.text: First, decide the constitutional question; second, declare the statute valid and end the case.
options.misconception: makes a validity ruling the required first step

options.text: First, read the statute broadly; second, decide the constitutional question only if the claim is pressed.
options.misconception: inverts avoidance into broad reading first

options.text: First, try the reading that avoids the conflict; second, reach the constitution only if no reading avoids it.

questions.explanation: A court tries a reasonable construction that avoids the constitutional conflict and decides the case on the statute, reaching the constitution only if no reading avoids it. Deciding the constitutional question first decides more than the case requires.
questions.hint: Statutory reading first, constitution only if forced.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: Identify the change most likely to remove any workable judicial standard
questions.stem: The atlas editor asks which change would most likely make a claim non-justiciable for lack of a workable standard.

options.text: The statute delegates the decision to an agency without supplying any rule for the court to apply.
The plaintiff filed the claim a year late, because delay affects the court's ability to decide.
options.misconception: makes timeliness a non-justiciability factor

options.text: The defendant is a state agency, because federal courts may not hear claims against states.
options.misconception: makes sovereign immunity the standard question

options.text: The claim is brought by a group of property owners, because group claims lack standards.
options.misconception: assumes group claims cannot be justiciable

questions.explanation: A delegation without any rule for the court to apply leaves the court without a manageable standard, which is what makes such claims non-justiciable. Delay, the defendant's identity, and multiple plaintiffs raise different questions.
questions.hint: No rule for the court to apply means no standard to apply.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a court treats a consent decree after its term expires
questions.stem: The records room asks how a court that entered a consent decree treats the decree once its stated term has expired.

answer.exemplar: Once the term expires, the obligations the decree imposed end by the decree's own force, and the court has no occasion to enforce terms that no longer bind. If the parties want different terms for the period after expiry, they must seek a new order, because the old decree no longer supplies an enforceable obligation to modify.

questions.explanation: An expired decree imposes nothing further, so there is nothing to enforce and nothing to modify. Continuing the arrangement requires a new order rather than reliance on terms that have lapsed.
questions.hint: Expired terms bind nobody and enforce nothing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conditions for availability of the writ of mandamus

stimulus.body: A guidance note states that a writ of mandamus issues only where the duty sought to be compelled is ministerial, that is, one the law leaves no discretion to the officer, and only where the petitioner has no other adequate remedy.

questions.stem: The guidance note supports which statement about the availability of the writ.

options.text: The writ is unavailable for a duty the law leaves to the officer's discretion, whatever the urgency.
The writ is available for any duty the officer has delayed, because delay always harms the petitioner.
options.misconception: makes delay the trigger for the writ

options.text: The writ is available whenever the petitioner shows the official is about to act unlawfully.
options.misconception: converts the writ into a preventive injunction

options.text: The writ is unavailable once the petitioner has filed any complaint with the agency.
options.misconception: makes any complaint defeat the writ

questions.explanation: A discretionary duty cannot be compelled by the writ, however urgent the petitioner's complaint. The note's two limits are the ministerial character of the duty and the absence of another adequate remedy.
questions.hint: Discretion is the limit the writ cannot cross.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a summary judgment ruling can stand where an affidavit creates dispute

stimulus.body: A claim note describes a case in which the defendant moved for summary judgment, the plaintiff produced an affidavit from a witness describing an oral agreement, and the court granted the motion without holding a hearing, noting that the affidavit raised a genuine dispute.

questions.stem: The translator asks what follows from the facts described in the note.

options.text: The court should not have granted the motion, because a hearing is required before judgment.
options.misconception: invents a hearing requirement for the motion

options.text: The court should have granted judgment for the plaintiff, because the affidavit proves the claim.
options.misconception: treats the affidavit as proof rather than as dispute

options.text: The court should have denied the motion, because a genuine dispute of material fact existed.
The ruling was correct, because the court may grant judgment whenever affidavits are filed.
options.misconception: treats any affidavit as sufficient for judgment

questions.explanation: A genuine dispute of material fact requires denial of the motion, so the court should not have granted judgment for the defendant. No hearing is required to decide the motion, and the affidavit is not proof of the claim but a source of dispute.
questions.hint: A genuine dispute blocks judgment on the papers.

questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the activist label asserts and how it is tested
questions.stem: The projection manual asks two things about a decision labelled activist: what the label asserts, and how it is tested.

options.text: It asserts the outcome was wrong; and it is tested by comparing the result with public opinion.
options.misconception: makes the label a verdict measured by opinion

options.text: It asserts the court lacked jurisdiction; and it is tested by counting the votes in the decision.
options.misconception: turns the label into a jurisdictional objection

options.text: It asserts the decision departed from precedent; and it is tested by counting the dissents.
options.misconception: measures activism by the number of dissents

options.text: It asserts the reasoning reached beyond the enacted law; and it is tested against the text and precedent.

questions.explanation: The label asserts that the court's reasoning reached beyond what the enacted law supports, and that assertion is tested against the text and the precedent. Outcome, jurisdiction, and vote counts are not what the charge concerns.
questions.hint: Test the charge against the words and the precedent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State how an overruled decision affects a later party who relies on it
questions.stem: A compiler asks how a court treats a decision that it has expressly overruled when a later party relies on it.

options.text: The later party is bound by the overruled decision, because the party reasonably relied on it.
options.misconception: makes reliance revive an overruled rule

options.text: The overruled decision does not control, though the court may consider the reliance in shaping relief.
The later party is bound by the new rule and may recover any loss the change caused.
options.misconception: turns reliance into a claim for damages

options.text: The earlier decision governs the later party, because reliance is a defence to the change of law.
options.misconception: treats reliance as a defence to overruling

questions.explanation: An overruled decision no longer controls, so a later party is bound by the new rule. The reliance may affect how relief is shaped, but it does not restore the old rule or create a claim for the loss caused.
questions.hint: Reliance shapes relief; it does not revive the rule.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court may not order relief binding non-parties
questions.stem: The survey office asks the reviewer to explain why a court may not order relief that benefits people who were not parties.

answer.exemplar: Because a court may only bind those who are before it, and the requirement of notice and an opportunity to be heard is a structural limit rather than a matter of convenience. Relief that runs against or binds a stranger would be made without any chance for that person to answer it, which is why the remedy must stay within the controversy and the parties.

questions.explanation: The limit on binding non-parties is structural, because a stranger has had no notice and no chance to be heard. Relief must therefore stay within the controversy and the parties before the court.
questions.hint: Nobody can be bound unheard.

questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Identify the trigger for the rule of constitutional avoidance

stimulus.body: A drafting note states that where a statute can reasonably be read in a way that avoids a constitutional difficulty, the court will adopt that reading and decide the case on the statute, and that the constitutional question is reached only where no reasonable construction avoids it.

questions.stem: The note states the governing approach for which of the following situations.

options.text: A case where the constitutional question has already been briefed by both parties.
options.misconception: makes briefing the trigger for the constitutional question

options.text: A case where the statute is open to a reasonable construction that avoids the constitutional problem.
A case where the legislature has expressed an intention about the constitutional limits of the statute.
options.misconception: makes legislative intent the trigger for constitutional review

options.text: A case where the court has doubts about the fairness of the statute's administration.
options.misconception: turns administrative fairness into constitutional avoidance

questions.explanation: The note describes a rule about construction, triggered by the availability of a reasonable reading that avoids the conflict. Briefing, legislative statements about limits, and doubts about administration are not the trigger.
questions.hint: The trigger is an available avoiding reading.

questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: Decide how a court treats a claim with no rule to apply

stimulus.body: A survey archive note describes a claim asking a court to decide how the executive branch should allocate funds among competing regional projects, and records that the court found no statutory rule that could guide the allocation.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the court in the scenario should treat the claim.

options.text: It should decide the claim, because courts may not decline to decide any dispute brought before them.
options.misconception: makes a duty to decide any dispute

options.text: It should dismiss the claim as moot, because the question will be answered by later legislation.
options.misconception: mislabels non-justiciability as mootness

options.text: It should remand the claim to the executive branch for a decision on the allocation.
options.misconception: treats the problem as an agency failure to decide

options.text: It should treat the claim as non-justiciable, because there is no standard to apply to the allocation.

questions.explanation: A claim with no rule to apply is non-justiciable, and the court declines to decide it while remaining within the separation of powers. A duty to decide every dispute, mootness, and remand are not the right frames for that problem.
questions.hint: No rule, so the court steps back.

questions.learningObjective: State what remains of a decree after its term and what continuing requires
questions.stem: The archivist asks two things about a consent decree whose term has run: what remains of it, and what a party must do to continue the arrangement.

options.text: Its obligations have ended; and the parties must obtain a new order if they want the arrangement to continue.
Its obligations have ended; and the parties may simply continue the arrangement on their own.
options.misconception: treats an expired decree as still self-executing

options.text: Its obligations remain in force; and the parties must apply to the court for an extension.
options.misconception: makes expiry extendable by the same decree

options.text: Its obligations remain in force; and the court retains power to enforce the old terms indefinitely.
options.misconception: makes enforcement survive the stated term

questions.explanation: When the term runs out the obligations end, and continuation requires a new order rather than the old decree or a private arrangement. The court does not retain indefinite power to enforce terms that have expired.
questions.hint: Expiry ends it; continuation needs a new order.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the factor that most clearly defeats a writ of mandamus
questions.stem: A projection clerk asks which factor most clearly prevents a writ of mandamus in a dispute about a permit.

options.text: The permit was refused orally, because a written refusal is needed to state a ministerial duty.
options.misconception: makes the form of the refusal decisive

options.text: The applicant waited six months, because delay alone defeats any petition for the writ.
options.misconception: makes delay an absolute bar to the writ

options.text: The statute gives the licensing board discretion over the conditions of the permit that was denied.
The applicant could have appealed the refusal, so another adequate remedy was available.
options.misconception: assumes an appeal always defeats the writ

questions.explanation: Discretion in the conditions of the permit means the duty sought is not ministerial, which is fatal to the writ. The form of the refusal, the length of the delay, and the availability of an appeal are not what decides the issue.
questions.hint: Look for the part the board still gets to choose.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a weak claim does not support judgment on the papers
questions.stem: The projection office asks why the court cannot enter judgment for the defendant merely because the plaintiff's claim looks weak on the papers.

answer.exemplar: Because judgment on the papers turns on a single question: whether the plaintiff has shown a genuine dispute of material fact. If the dispute is genuine, the claim must be resolved by a fact-finder, and the court may neither weigh the evidence nor assess credibility. Weakness of the claim is for the trial, and allowing it to drive judgment would replace that role with the judge's impression.

questions.explanation: The single question on the papers is whether a genuine dispute of material fact exists, not whether the claim looks weak. Letting weakness drive judgment would substitute the judge's impression for the fact-finder's work.
questions.hint: One question only, and it is not who looks stronger.

questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Identify the nature of the activist and restrained labels

stimulus.body: A marginal note in the archive explains that a decision may be criticised as activist where its reasoning departs from the enacted text, and criticised as restrained where its reasoning stretches the text further than the legislature's words support, and that the two are argued case by case.

questions.stem: The note indicates that the labels are best understood as which of the following.

options.text: Fixed categories assigned to panels, so that each court has a known reputation in the debate.
options.misconception: makes the labels fixed reputations of courts

options.text: Choices a court makes about remedies, so that the label depends on the relief granted.
options.misconception: ties the labels to the remedy granted

options.text: Descriptions of the speed of decision, since a prompt ruling is thought to be the bolder one.
options.misconception: turns the labels into a measure of speed

options.text: Arguments about construction that must be made from the text and precedent in each case.

questions.explanation: The labels are arguments about how far the court went in construing the text, and they must be made case by case from the opinion and the precedent. They are not panel reputations, remedial choices, or measures of speed.
questions.hint: Read the note for how the labels must be used.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between overruling and reliance on the earlier rule

stimulus.body: An atlas note records that a court overruled an earlier decision, observed that surveyors had relied on the earlier line for many years, and explained that the change would apply to future surveys while leaving the boundaries already established in place.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the note shows about the relationship between overruling and reliance.

options.text: That the court was bound to preserve the old line forever, because reliance was so widespread.
options.misconception: makes widespread reliance a bar to overruling

options.text: That the change of law operates on future cases, with completed work in reliance on the old rule preserved.
That the new rule governs only future cases and has no effect on the case being decided.
options.misconception: excludes the case before the court from the new rule

options.text: That the earlier line survives because the surveyors who relied on it outnumbered those who did not.
options.misconception: makes reliance a matter of numbers

questions.explanation: The note shows the ordinary operation of an overrule, where the new rule governs the case and later cases while completed work in reliance on the old rule is preserved. Reliance is a reason to explain the change, not to refuse it.
questions.hint: New rule forward, established boundaries stay.

questions.learningObjective: State the reach of relief where several landowners are involved

options.text: It may grant relief that binds the parties and concerns the lands in dispute; and it may not reach the other owners.
It may grant relief that binds the parties and concerns the lands in dispute; and it may reach any owner it chooses.
options.misconception: allows the court to reach owners at will

options.text: It may grant relief that binds every owner of adjoining land; and it may do so once they are notified.
options.misconception: treats notice to non-parties as sufficient to bind them

options.text: It may grant relief only in the parties' own favour; and it may not touch the disputed boundary at all.
options.misconception: makes a remedial restriction that the doctrine does not impose

questions.explanation: Relief binds the parties and addresses the lands in the controversy, and it cannot reach the other owners who were not before the court. Notice alone does not bring them within the judgment, and relief is not confined to what favours the parties.
questions.hint: Parties and disputed lands only.

questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: State when a court should decide a case on the statute alone
questions.stem: A grid note asks when a court should decline to decide a constitutional question and resolve the case on the statute instead.

options.text: When the constitutional question is difficult, because hard questions deserve fuller argument.
options.misconception: makes difficulty the trigger for avoidance

options.text: When the statute has already been interpreted by a court, because interpretation settles everything.
options.misconception: makes prior construction settle the constitution

options.text: When a reasonable construction of the statute would avoid the constitutional problem entirely.
When the plaintiff has failed to exhaust other remedies, because the case is not yet ready.
options.misconception: ties avoidance to exhaustion

questions.explanation: The court avoids the constitutional question when a reasonable construction of the statute resolves the case without it. Difficulty, prior interpretation, and exhaustion are separate matters that do not trigger the doctrine.
questions.hint: An available avoiding reading is the trigger.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the political question doctrine is used sparingly
questions.stem: The cartographer asks why the doctrine of political questions is used sparingly by courts.

answer.exemplar: Because the label carries a serious consequence: the claim is dismissed and the person who brought it is left without a remedy. Courts are therefore reluctant to find a question non-justiciable unless the absence of a workable standard is clear, whether because the constitution commits the matter to another branch or because a statutory standard is too indefinite to apply.

questions.explanation: The consequence of the label is dismissal without a remedy, so courts require a clear absence of any workable standard before invoking it. Sensitivity, timing, and convenience are not enough.
questions.hint: The cost of getting it wrong is a dismissed claim.

questions.hint: The clause dates the ending of the obligations.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an overruled decision still governs the cases decided under it
questions.stem: The compiler asks the reviewer to explain why the law does not treat an overruled decision as having governed the earlier cases.

answer.exemplar: Because overruling changes the rule for the future, and it does not undo what was lawfully done while the earlier rule stood. A judgment already entered and work completed in reliance on the old rule are treated as settled, so that parties are not punished for acting on the law as it was. The earlier cases therefore remain the products of the rule that governed them at the time.

questions.explanation: An overrule operates prospectively, so earlier judgments and completed work stay settled and parties are not punished for acting on the law as it then stood. The earlier cases were the product of the rule that governed them.
questions.hint: The rule that governed them stays the rule that judged them.

questions.stem: The annotation indicates that the clause in the judgment accomplishes which of the following.

options.text: It extends the court's authority to anyone claiming an interest in the same boundary line.
options.misconception: reads the clause as an extension of authority

options.text: It makes the judgment void, because a court may not limit the effect of its own orders.
options.misconception: treats a limiting clause as invalidating the judgment

options.text: It confines the judgment to the parties, consistent with the requirement that a court bind only those before it.
It requires the plaintiffs to notify every other owner before the boundary may be marked.
options.misconception: adds a notification duty to the clause

questions.explanation: The clause confines the judgment to the parties, which is what the structural limits require. It neither extends the court's authority to non-parties nor invalidates the judgment, and it imposes no notification requirement.
questions.hint: Read the clause for who is affected.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case
questions.learningObjective: Decide how a court should proceed where a statute has two possible readings

stimulus.body: A projection record describes a statute that prohibits one thing in terms broad enough to reach two different activities, and a note observes that a narrower reading would confine it to one activity and avoid any question about the other.

questions.stem: The translator asks how the court should proceed in the situation described.

options.text: It should decide the constitutional question first, because the broader reading is the statute's plain meaning.
options.misconception: makes plain meaning override the avoidance rule

options.text: It should invalidate the statute, because a statute that can be read two ways is inherently suspect.
options.misconception: makes ambiguity a ground for invalidation

options.text: It should declare the statute ambiguous and stop, because it cannot choose between the readings.
options.misconception: makes ambiguity a reason to decide nothing

options.text: It should adopt the narrower reading if reasonable and resolve the case on the statute alone.

questions.explanation: Where a narrower reading is reasonable and avoids the constitutional question, the court adopts it and decides the case on the statute. Plain meaning at the broadest level, invalidation, and declaring ambiguity do not displace that approach.
questions.hint: Take the reading that avoids the constitutional question.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard
questions.learningObjective: State the reason and the consequence for a non-justiciable claim
questions.stem: The drafting room asks two things about a claim the court treats as non-justiciable: what makes it so, and what the court does with it.

options.text: There is no standard to apply; and the court declines to decide the claim and dismisses it.
The claim is weak on the merits; and the court dismisses it for failure to state a claim.
options.misconception: makes non-justiciability a pleading defect

options.text: The agency has not decided; and the court remands the claim for an agency decision.
options.misconception: turns the standard question into a remand

options.text: There is no standard to apply; and the court decides the claim anyway on the best available standard.
options.misconception: invents a standard where none exists

questions.explanation: The court treats the claim as non-justiciable because no workable standard exists, and it declines to decide the claim and dismisses it. A weak claim, agency inaction, and inventing a standard are not the governing frames.
questions.hint: No standard, so the claim is dismissed unresolved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify why the entering court handles a request to end a decree early
questions.stem: A custodian asks why the same court that entered a consent decree is the one that usually handles a request to end it early.

options.text: Because only the entering court can ever enforce any order, so all changes must go there.
options.misconception: makes enforcement the reason for the exclusive forum

options.text: Because the decree was entered by that court and the continuing power to adjust it rests with it.
Because the parties agreed in the decree that no other court could hear any dispute about it.
options.misconception: assumes a forum clause without support

options.text: Because a decree is a contract, and contracts may be modified only where it was signed.
options.misconception: reduces a decree to a private contract

questions.explanation: The power to modify or dissolve a consent decree belongs to the court that entered it, because that court entered the judgment and retained jurisdiction over it. A forum clause and the contract analogy are not what decide the question.
questions.hint: The decree is that court's own judgment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a ministerial duty from a discretionary one
questions.stem: The survey handbook asks the reviewer to distinguish a ministerial duty from a discretionary one.

answer.exemplar: A ministerial duty is one where the governing law leaves the officer no room to choose: once the stated conditions are met, the act is required and the method is fixed. A discretionary duty involves judgment or choice among lawful options, and the officer may lawfully select among them. Because a court may not control the exercise of discretion, only ministerial duties can be compelled by a writ of mandamus.

questions.explanation: The distinction turns on whether the governing law leaves the officer any choice at all. Since a court cannot control the exercise of discretion, only a duty that is fixed once its conditions are met can be compelled by the writ.
questions.hint: Is there any choice left once the conditions are met?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the evidence requirement for judgment for the defendant

stimulus.body: A note for junior staff states that a court may enter summary judgment for the defendant only where the plaintiff has failed to produce evidence that would permit a reasonable person to find for the plaintiff, that the court must take the plaintiff's evidence as true, and that allegations alone are not evidence.

questions.stem: The note supports which statement about judgment for the defendant.

options.text: The defendant wins whenever the plaintiff's allegations are not proven beyond doubt.
options.misconception: sets a criminal standard for the motion

options.text: The defendant wins whenever the court thinks the plaintiff would probably lose the trial.
options.misconception: replaces the test with the judge's probability view

options.text: The defendant wins only where the plaintiff has failed to show evidence that a reasonable person could credit.
The defendant wins whenever the plaintiff has failed to respond to the motion in time.
options.misconception: treats default as decisive on the merits

questions.explanation: The note states the test as the absence of evidence a reasonable person could credit in the plaintiff's favour, with allegations alone insufficient. A heightened standard, a probability view, and a missed response are not the test.
questions.hint: What must the plaintiff have put before the court?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a disagreement between commentators over the labels shows

stimulus.body: A margin note records a decision that enforced a statute according to its plain terms and was described by one commentator as restrained and by another as activist because it declined to read the statute in a way the commentator preferred.

questions.stem: The translator asks what the disagreement in the scenario shows.

options.text: That the labels are meaningless, because the same ruling can carry opposite descriptions.
options.misconception: concludes that the labels are meaningless

options.text: That the labels are arguments about construction that each commentator must support with the text.
That the ruling was wrongly decided, because two commentators cannot both be right.
options.misconception: treats disagreement as proof of error

options.text: That the court should state expressly whether its ruling is activist or restrained.
options.misconception: invites a self-labeling requirement for courts

questions.explanation: The disagreement shows the labels are contestable arguments about construction, so each commentator has to point to the text and the precedent. Disagreement does not prove the ruling wrong, and courts are not required to classify themselves.
questions.hint: Each commentator has to make the argument.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the operation of a change of rule and its effect on completed acts
questions.stem: The projection compiler asks two things about a change of rule: what it does to the law now, and what it does to completed acts.

options.text: It changes the law for future cases; and it invalidates any act done under the earlier rule.
options.misconception: makes the change undo completed reliance

options.text: It changes the law for future cases; and it leaves completed acts done under the earlier rule undisturbed.
It changes nothing at all; and it merely announces what the court now believes about the old rule.
options.misconception: makes the announcement a change without effect

options.text: It changes the law for all cases; and it preserves acts done after the announcement only.
options.misconception: confuses the direction of the rule's operation

questions.explanation: A change of rule operates on cases that come after it and leaves completed acts under the earlier rule undisturbed. An announcement that changes nothing is not an overrule, and the direction of operation is not reversed by the timing of acts.
questions.hint: Forward for the law, backward for completed acts.
